assessment.title: Initial English Diagnostic A1–C2
assessment.description: An adaptive placement diagnostic that estimates your starting level across Grammar & Use of English, Vocabulary, Reading, and Listening.
assessment.instructions: Answer each stage without external help. The diagnostic begins at B1 and selects the next level from your responses. Listening passages may be played a maximum of two times.

questions.prompt: Complete: My name ___ Daniel.
questions.explanation: Use "is" with a singular third-person subject.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
questions.explanation: "She" is the subject pronoun.

questions.prompt: Complete: I have ___ umbrella.
questions.explanation: Use "an" before a vowel sound.

questions.prompt: Complete: Tom ___ to work at eight every day.
questions.explanation: Present simple third-person singular takes -s/-es.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
questions.explanation: Use can + base verb.

questions.prompt: Complete: They ___ dinner now.
questions.explanation: Present continuous describes an action happening now.

questions.prompt: Which phrase describes a daily routine?
questions.explanation: Getting up at a regular time is a routine.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct phrase.
questions.explanation: Use "on" with days.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
questions.explanation: Use "there are" with plural nouns.

questions.prompt: Which is the most natural response to "How are you?"
questions.explanation: This is a standard response to a greeting question.

questions.prompt: Complete: We ___ the museum yesterday.
questions.explanation: Use past simple for a finished past event.

questions.prompt: Past form of "take":
questions.explanation: "Take" is irregular: take → took.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct question.
questions.explanation: Use did + subject + base verb.

questions.prompt: This apartment is ___ than the other one.
questions.explanation: Use the comparative "larger".

questions.prompt: They are going to ___ next weekend.
questions.explanation: Use going to + base verb.

questions.prompt: Complete: She has never ___ sushi.
questions.explanation: Present perfect uses the past participle.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct phrase.
questions.explanation: Use "many" with plural countable nouns.

questions.prompt: Adverb form of "careful":
questions.explanation: "Carefully" is the adverb.

questions.prompt: Which sentence gives advice?
questions.explanation: "Should" is commonly used for advice.

questions.prompt: What does "get off the bus" mean?
questions.explanation: "Get off" means leave a bus/train.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
questions.option_a: I have visited Rome last year.
questions.option_c: I have visit Rome last year.
questions.option_d: I did visited Rome last year.
questions.explanation: A finished past time takes past simple.

questions.prompt: She has worked here ___ 2022.
questions.explanation: Use "since" with a starting point.

questions.prompt: I ___ home when I ___ the accident.
questions.explanation: Background action + shorter past event.

questions.prompt: If it ___ tomorrow, we will stay home.
questions.explanation: First conditional uses present simple after if.

questions.prompt: If I ___ more time, I would learn Italian.
questions.explanation: Second conditional uses past simple in the if-clause.

questions.prompt: The bridge ___ in 2008.
questions.explanation: Past passive uses was/were + past participle.

questions.prompt: Which phrase means there is no necessity?
questions.explanation: "Do not have to" means optional/not necessary.

questions.prompt: What does "run out of" mean?
questions.explanation: It means use all of something so none remains.

questions.prompt: Which linker shows contrast?
questions.explanation: "However" signals contrast.

questions.prompt: Which relative pronoun normally refers to people?
questions.explanation: "Who" refers to people.

questions.prompt: By the time we arrived, the presentation ___.
questions.explanation: Past perfect marks the earlier past event.

questions.prompt: I ___ on this report all morning.
questions.explanation: Present perfect continuous emphasizes duration.

questions.prompt: By Friday, we ___ the migration.
questions.explanation: Future perfect marks completion before a future point.

questions.prompt: If I had known, I ___ you.
questions.explanation: Third conditional result: would have + participle.

questions.prompt: The office is empty. Everyone ___ home.
questions.explanation: Must have + participle expresses strong past deduction.

questions.prompt: Report: "Where do you work?"
questions.option_b: She asked where did I work.
questions.option_c: She asked where do I work.
questions.option_d: She asked me where worked I.
questions.explanation: Reported questions use statement word order.

questions.prompt: What does "look into a problem" mean?
questions.explanation: "Look into" means investigate.

questions.prompt: Which connector means "despite that" or "however"?
questions.explanation: "Nevertheless" signals contrast/concession.

questions.prompt: Choose the natural collocation.
questions.explanation: "Make progress" is the standard collocation.

questions.prompt: Which is most appropriate in a formal request?
questions.option_a: I would appreciate it if you could respond by Friday.
questions.explanation: The first option matches formal professional register.

questions.prompt: Not until the report was published ___ the scale of the problem.
questions.explanation: Negative/restrictive fronting triggers inversion.

questions.prompt: ___ surprised me most was the lack of preparation.
questions.explanation: A what-clause creates a pseudo-cleft.

questions.prompt: ___ you require further information, please contact us.
questions.explanation: Formal conditional inversion uses "Should you require...".

questions.prompt: ___ the evidence, the committee revised its recommendation.
questions.explanation: Perfect participle shows prior completion.

questions.prompt: The minister is thought ___ the proposal last week.
questions.explanation: Perfect infinitive reports an earlier action.

questions.prompt: Several delegates, many of ___ were experts, attended.
questions.explanation: Quantifier + whom is a formal relative structure.

questions.prompt: Which phrase most clearly hedges a claim?
questions.explanation: "Appears to suggest" reduces commitment.

questions.prompt: What is "a grey area"?
questions.explanation: A grey area is unclear or not fully defined.

questions.prompt: "You might want to check those figures again" most likely implies...
questions.option_a: the figures may contain an error
questions.explanation: It is a tactful suggestion/criticism.

questions.prompt: What does a rebuttal do?
questions.explanation: A rebuttal addresses a counterargument.

questions.prompt: Why might a speaker say "I was hoping you could help"?
questions.option_b: to locate help only in the past
questions.explanation: Past progressive can create interpersonal distance and politeness.

questions.prompt: In "The results should be available tomorrow," "should" expresses...
questions.explanation: At advanced level, should can mark expectation.

questions.prompt: She predicted the system would fail, and ___ it did.
questions.explanation: "So it did" emphatically confirms the prediction.

questions.prompt: The current findings are stronger than ___ of the pilot study.
questions.explanation: "Those" substitutes for plural findings.

questions.prompt: Which paraphrase preserves "may contribute"?
questions.explanation: The cautious causal meaning is preserved.

questions.prompt: In "Although the evidence is limited, the findings suggest a pattern," the main clause is...
questions.explanation: The although-clause is subordinate.

questions.prompt: Which word best means a limiting condition that does not necessarily make action impossible?
questions.explanation: A constraint limits options.

questions.prompt: If a proposal "gains traction," it...
questions.explanation: The metaphor means increasing acceptance.

questions.prompt: After a serious failure, "That was not exactly ideal" is usually...
questions.explanation: The phrase minimizes wording while implying criticism.

questions.prompt: Which issue can a voluntary survey create?
questions.explanation: Volunteers may differ systematically from non-respondents.

passages.title: A Typical Morning
passages.instructions: Read the passage carefully and answer the four questions.
passages.content_text: Emma gets up at seven o’clock every weekday. She has breakfast in the kitchen and drinks tea. At eight, she walks to the bus stop. She works in a small shop near the city center. The shop opens at nine. Emma likes her job because she talks to many people during the day.

questions.prompt: What time does Emma get up?
questions.explanation: She gets up at seven.

questions.prompt: What does she drink at breakfast?
questions.explanation: The text says she drinks tea.

questions.prompt: How does she go to the bus stop?
questions.explanation: She walks to the bus stop.

questions.prompt: Why does Emma like her job?
questions.explanation: She likes interacting with people.

passages.title: At the Café
passages.instructions: Listen to the passage and answer the four questions. You may play the audio twice.
passages.audio_text: Good morning. Can I have a cheese sandwich and a cup of tea, please? Of course. Would you like milk in your tea? Yes, please, but no sugar. Anything else? No, thank you. That is all.

questions.prompt: What food does the customer order?
questions.explanation: The customer orders a cheese sandwich.

questions.prompt: What drink does the customer order?
questions.explanation: The customer asks for tea.

questions.prompt: Does the customer want milk?
questions.explanation: The customer says yes to milk.

questions.prompt: Does the customer want sugar?
questions.explanation: The customer says no sugar.

passages.title: A Weekend Change of Plan
passages.instructions: Read the passage carefully and answer the four questions.
passages.content_text: Leo planned to visit his cousin on Saturday, but his train was canceled. He called his cousin and explained the problem. Instead of traveling, Leo stayed in town and met two friends for lunch. In the afternoon, they went to a free exhibition at the local museum. Leo was disappointed about the canceled trip, but he still enjoyed the day. He is going to visit his cousin next weekend instead.

questions.prompt: Why did Leo not visit his cousin?
questions.explanation: The train cancellation changed the plan.

questions.prompt: What did Leo do for lunch?
questions.explanation: He met two friends for lunch.

questions.prompt: How did Leo feel about the canceled trip?
questions.explanation: The text says he was disappointed.

questions.prompt: What is Leo going to do next weekend?
questions.explanation: He plans to visit his cousin next weekend.

passages.title: Train Information
passages.instructions: Listen to the passage and answer the four questions. You may play the audio twice.
passages.audio_text: Excuse me, what time is the next train to Bristol? The next direct train leaves at eleven twenty from platform four. Does it stop in Bath? No, it goes directly to Bristol. If you need Bath, there is another train at eleven forty-five from platform six.

questions.prompt: What time is the direct train to Bristol?
questions.explanation: The direct train leaves at 11:20.

questions.prompt: Which platform does it use?
questions.explanation: It leaves from platform four.

questions.prompt: Does the direct Bristol train stop in Bath?
questions.explanation: It goes directly to Bristol.

questions.prompt: Which platform is used for the Bath train?
questions.explanation: The Bath service leaves from platform six.

passages.title: A New Way of Commuting
passages.instructions: Read the passage carefully and answer the four questions.
passages.content_text: For years, Maya drove to work every day. The journey usually took about forty minutes, but traffic was getting worse. Last spring, her company introduced secure bicycle parking and showers for employees. Maya decided to try cycling twice a week. At first, she found the journey tiring, especially on the hills. After a few weeks, however, it became easier. She has now been cycling for six months and says she arrives at work feeling more awake. She still drives when the weather is bad or when she needs to carry heavy equipment.

questions.prompt: Why did Maya consider changing how she traveled?
questions.explanation: Increasing traffic motivated the change.

questions.prompt: What support did her company introduce?
questions.explanation: Those facilities made cycling easier.

questions.prompt: How has cycling changed over time for Maya?
questions.explanation: The initial difficulty reduced with practice.

questions.prompt: When does she still drive?
questions.option_a: In bad weather or with heavy equipment
questions.explanation: She keeps the car for specific circumstances.

passages.title: Changing a Meeting
passages.instructions: Listen to the passage and answer the four questions. You may play the audio twice.
passages.audio_text: Hi, Sara. I am calling about tomorrow’s meeting. The client cannot make ten o’clock, so they have asked if we can move it to the afternoon. I am free after two. Could we meet at three thirty? That works for me. I will update the calendar and send the client the new invitation.

questions.prompt: Why must the meeting move?
questions.option_a: The client cannot attend at ten.
questions.explanation: The client cannot make the original time.

questions.prompt: When is the speaker free?
questions.explanation: The speaker says they are free after two.

questions.prompt: What new time do they choose?
questions.explanation: They agree on 3:30.

questions.prompt: What will happen next?
questions.option_a: The calendar will be updated and a new invitation sent.
questions.explanation: The speaker will update the calendar and invitation.

passages.title: A Four-Day Week Trial
passages.instructions: Read the passage carefully and answer the four questions.
passages.content_text: A medium-sized design company recently completed a six-month trial of a four-day working week. Employees worked fewer hours without a reduction in salary, but teams were expected to maintain the same level of service. According to the company, project deadlines were met at roughly the same rate as before, while reported job satisfaction increased. However, the trial also exposed difficulties. Some client-facing teams struggled to provide coverage on Fridays, and several managers said meetings became harder to schedule. The company has decided to continue the arrangement for another six months, but it will modify staffing patterns before making a permanent decision.

questions.prompt: What remained roughly unchanged during the trial?
questions.option_a: The rate at which deadlines were met
questions.explanation: Deadline performance remained similar.

questions.prompt: What improved according to the company?
questions.explanation: Employees reported higher satisfaction.

questions.prompt: What difficulty did client-facing teams experience?
questions.explanation: Coverage on Fridays was a challenge.

questions.prompt: Why has the company not made the change permanent yet?
questions.option_a: It wants another trial with modifications.
questions.option_d: Clients demanded five days by law.
questions.explanation: The company wants more evidence after adjusting staffing.

passages.title: Implementation Review
passages.instructions: Listen to the passage and answer the four questions. You may play the audio twice.
passages.audio_text: Overall, the new process is working reasonably well, but there are two areas we need to address. First, approval times have improved, although not as much as we expected. Second, staff are still entering the same information into two systems. If we can remove that duplication, we should see a more significant improvement. I suggest we keep the process for another month and review the data again before making any further changes.

questions.prompt: What has improved?
questions.explanation: Approval times have improved.

questions.prompt: What problem remains?
questions.explanation: Staff enter the same information twice.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker expect if duplication is removed?
questions.explanation: Removing duplication should improve results.

questions.prompt: What is recommended?
questions.option_a: Continue for another month and review again
questions.explanation: The speaker recommends more observation before further change.

passages.title: Interpreting a Policy Evaluation
passages.instructions: Read the passage carefully and answer the four questions.
passages.content_text: An evaluation of a new housing-support program found that participants were more likely to remain in stable accommodation after twelve months than people who had applied before the program existed. At first sight, the result appears compelling. However, the two groups were drawn from different periods, during which rental prices and employment conditions also changed. The authors acknowledge that these wider economic differences may have influenced the outcome. They therefore stop short of claiming that the program alone caused the improvement. Instead, they argue that the findings are consistent with a positive effect and justify a more rigorous follow-up study.

questions.prompt: Why is a simple causal conclusion problematic?
questions.option_a: The groups came from different economic periods.
questions.explanation: Other changes may have affected outcomes.

questions.prompt: How do the authors characterize the evidence?
questions.option_a: Consistent with a positive effect but not conclusive
questions.option_b: Proof that the program caused all improvement
questions.explanation: They hedge the causal interpretation.

questions.prompt: What do the authors recommend?
questions.explanation: They see enough promise to justify stronger research.

questions.prompt: What is the writer doing by saying "At first sight"?
questions.option_a: Signaling that the initial interpretation needs qualification
questions.explanation: The phrase prepares the reader for a more nuanced interpretation.

passages.title: Polite Disagreement
passages.instructions: Listen to the passage and answer the four questions. You may play the audio twice.
passages.audio_text: I can see why the proposal is attractive, particularly from a cost perspective. I am not entirely convinced, though, that we have allowed enough time for user testing. We could probably launch on the proposed date, but doing so would leave very little room to respond if the final tests reveal anything unexpected. I would be more comfortable with a two-week delay.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker acknowledge positively?
questions.option_a: The proposal is attractive on cost grounds
questions.explanation: The speaker concedes the cost advantage.

questions.prompt: What is the main reservation?
questions.explanation: The speaker doubts the testing timeline.

questions.prompt: Does the speaker think the proposed launch date is impossible?
questions.option_c: The speaker does not discuss it.
questions.explanation: The speaker says they could probably launch but with little margin.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker prefer?
questions.explanation: The preference is stated directly.

passages.title: When Measurement Changes the Thing Measured
passages.instructions: Read the passage carefully and answer the four questions.
passages.content_text: Performance indicators are often introduced to make organizations more accountable. Yet once a measure becomes consequential, people adapt their behavior to it. A hospital judged primarily by waiting times may reduce queues in ways that improve efficiency, but it may also redirect attention from aspects of care that are harder to quantify. This does not make measurement useless. It does mean that indicators can become part of the system they are intended merely to observe. The most sophisticated evaluation frameworks therefore treat metrics not as neutral mirrors of performance but as interventions that influence priorities, incentives, and sometimes even the definition of success itself.

questions.prompt: What central paradox does the passage identify?
questions.option_a: Measures can influence the behavior they measure.
questions.explanation: Consequential measures alter incentives and behavior.

questions.prompt: Does the writer reject performance indicators?
questions.option_a: No, but the writer rejects treating them as neutral.
questions.explanation: The argument is qualified rather than dismissive.

questions.prompt: What does "neutral mirrors" imply?
questions.option_a: Measures that merely reflect reality without affecting it
questions.explanation: The metaphor contrasts passive observation with active influence.

questions.prompt: What is the most sophisticated evaluation approach according to the passage?
questions.option_a: Treat metrics as interventions as well as measurements
questions.option_d: Measure only what is easy to quantify
questions.explanation: The passage explicitly recommends this broader interpretation.

passages.title: Interpreting Mixed Evidence
passages.instructions: Listen to the passage and answer the four questions. You may play the audio twice.
passages.audio_text: I would resist the temptation to call these findings contradictory. The first study measures short-term output, whereas the second looks at error rates over a full year. So they are not really asking the same question. What is interesting is that both suggest the intervention changes performance, but possibly in different ways at different times. The sensible next step is not to decide which study is right; it is to design research that can test both patterns within the same framework.

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker resist calling the studies contradictory?
questions.option_a: They measure different outcomes and time frames
questions.explanation: They are not asking exactly the same question.

questions.prompt: What do both studies suggest broadly?
questions.explanation: The speaker identifies a shared broad implication.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker reject as the next step?
questions.explanation: The speaker argues against a winner-takes-all interpretation.

questions.prompt: What research approach is recommended?
questions.option_a: Test both patterns in the same framework
questions.explanation: The speaker wants a design that can evaluate both findings together.
